danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: Marja Dmitrijevna, der havde fundet Sonja grædende ude i gangen, fik hende til at tilstå alt, og efter at have opsnappet sedlen til Natasja læste hun den og gik ind til Natasjas værelse med den i hånden.
»Din skamløse tøs!« sagde hun. »Jeg vil ikke høre et ord.«

Hun skubbede Natasja, der så på hende med forbavsede men tåreløse øjne, til side, låste hende inde; og efter at have givet ordre til gårdvagten om at lukke de personer ind, der ville komme den aften, men ikke lade dem gå igen, og beordret lakajen at bringe dem op til hende, satte hun sig i salonen for at vente på bortførerne.

Da Gabriel kom for at meddele hende, at mændene, der var kommet, var flygtet igen, rejste hun sig med rynkede bryn og gik med hænderne knyttet bag ryggen frem og tilbage gennem rummene og overvejede længe, hvad hun skulle gøre. Hen mod midnat gik hun til Natasjas værelse og fingerede ved nøglen i lommen. Sonja sad og hulkede i gangen. »Marja Dmitrijevna, lad mig for Guds skyld komme ind til hende!« bad hun, men Marja Dmitrijevna låste døren op og gik ind uden at svare hende... »Modbydeligt, afskyeligt... I mit hus... frygtelig pige, tøs! Jeg har kun ondt af hendes far!« tænkte hun og forsøgte at tøjle sin vrede. »Hvor svært det end bliver, skal jeg sige til dem alle, at de skal tie stille, og skjule det for greven.« Hun trådte ind i værelset med beslutsomme skridt. Natasja lå på sofaen med hovedet skjult i hænderne og rørte sig ikke. Hun lå i nøjagtig den stilling, Marja Dmitrijevna havde efterladt hende i.

»En pæn pige! Rigtig pæn!« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna. »Arrangerer stævnemøder med elskere i mit hus! Det nytter ikke at lade som ingenting: du skal høre, hvad jeg siger!« Og Marja Dmitrijevna rørte ved hendes arm. »Hør, når jeg taler! Du har vanæret dig selv som den laveste tøjte. Jeg ville behandle dig anderledes, men jeg har medlidenhed med din far, så jeg holder det skjult.«
Natasja ændrede ikke stilling, men hele hendes krop rystede af lydløse, krampeagtige hulk, der kvalte hende. Marja Dmitrijevna kiggede sig omkring, satte sig på sofaen ved siden af Natasja.
»Han er heldig, at han slap fra mig; men jeg finder ham nok!« sagde hun med sin ru stemme. »Hører du, hvad jeg siger, eller ej?« tilføjede hun.

Hun lagde sin store hånd under Natasjas ansigt og vendte det mod sig. Både Marja Dmitrijevna og Sonja blev forbløffede, da de så, hvordan Natasja så ud. Hendes øjne var tørre og glinsende, hendes læber sammenpressede, hendes kinder indfaldne.
»Lad mig være!... Hvad rager det mig?... Jeg skal dø!« mumlede hun og rev sig løs fra Marja Dmitrijevnas hænder med en ond bevægelse og sank ned i sin tidligere stilling.

»Natalja!« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna. »Jeg vil dit bedste. Bliv liggende, bliv sådan, så rører jeg dig ikke. Men lyt. Jeg vil ikke fortælle dig, hvor skyldig du er. Det ved du selv. Men når din far kommer hjem i morgen, hvad skal jeg så fortælle ham? Hvad?«
Igen rystede Natasjas krop af hulk.
»Tænk, hvis han finder ud af det, og din bror og din forlovede?«
»Jeg har ingen forlovede: Jeg har afvist ham!« råbte Natasja.
»Det er det samme,« fortsatte Marja Dmitrijevna. »Hvis de hører om det, tror du så, de lader det gå? Han, din far — jeg kender ham... hvis han udfordrer ham til duel, bliver det så godt? Hvad?«
»Åh, lad mig være! Hvorfor har du blandet dig? Hvorfor? Hvorfor? Hvem bad dig om det?« råbte Natasja, idet hun rejste sig op på sofaen og så ondsindet på Marja Dmitrijevna.

»Men hvad ville du?« råbte Marja Dmitrijevna og blev igen vred. »Blev du holdt under lås og slå? Hvem hindrede ham i at komme i huset? Hvorfor bortføre dig, som om du var en sigøjnersangerinde?... Nå, hvis han havde bortført dig... tror du ikke, de ville have fundet ham? Din far, eller bror, eller din forlovede? Og han er en slyngel, en usling — det er en kendsgerning!«
»Han er bedre end nogen af jer!« udbrød Natasja og rejste sig op. »Hvis I ikke havde blandet jer... Åh, Gud! Hvad er det hele? Hvad er det? Sonja, hvorfor?... Gå væk!«
Og hun brast i gråd med den fortvivlede heftighed, hvormed mennesker begræder ulykker, de føler, de selv har forvoldt. Marja Dmitrijevna ville tale igen, men Natasja råbte:
»Gå væk! Gå væk! I hader mig alle og foragter mig!« og hun kastede sig tilbage på sofaen.

Marja Dmitrijevna blev ved med at formane hende i nogen tid, indskærpede, at det hele måtte holdes skjult for hendes far, og forsikrede hende om, at ingen ville få noget at vide, hvis blot Natasja selv påtog sig at glemme det hele og ikke lade nogen se, at noget var hændt. Natasja svarede ikke og hulkede heller ikke længere, men hun blev kold og fik kuldegysninger. Marja Dmitrijevna lagde en pude under hendes hoved, lagde to dyner over hende og bragte selv noget lindeblomstvand, men Natasja reagerede ikke.
»Nå, lad hende sove,« sagde Marja Dmitrijevna, da hun gik ud af værelset i den tro, at Natasja sov.
Men Natasja sov ikke; med blegt ansigt og stivt stirrende øjne så hun lige ud. Hele natten sov hun ikke, græd ikke og talte ikke til Sonja, der rejste sig og gik hen til hende flere gange.

Næste dag vendte grev Rostov hjem fra sit gods nær Moskva til frokost som lovet. Han var i meget godt humør; handelen med køberen gik tilfredsstillende, og der var intet, der holdt ham længere i Moskva, borte fra grevinden, som han savnede. Marja Dmitrijevna mødte ham og fortalte, at Natasja havde været meget dårlig dagen før, og at de havde sendt bud efter lægen, men at hun nu havde det bedre. Natasja havde ikke forladt sit værelse den morgen. Med sammenpressede, udtørrede læber og tørre, stirrende øjne sad hun ved vinduet og fulgte uroligt de mennesker, der kørte forbi, og så hastigt om sig efter enhver, der trådte ind i rummet. Hun ventede tydeligvis nyt fra ham og at han ville komme eller skrive til hende.

Da greven kom ind for at se til hende, vendte hun sig uroligt om ved lyden af mandlige fodtrin, og så genoptog hendes ansigt sit kolde og ondsindede udtryk. Hun rejste sig ikke engang for at hilse på ham. »Hvad er der i vejen med dig, min engel? Er du syg?« spurgte greven.
Efter et øjebliks tavshed svarede Natasja: »Ja, syg.«

På grevens urolige spørgsmål om, hvorfor hun var så nedtrykt, og om noget var hændt med hendes forlovede, forsikrede hun ham om, at intet var sket, og bad ham ikke bekymre sig. Marja Dmitrijevna bekræftede Natasjas forsikringer om, at intet var sket. Af den foregivne sygdom, hans datters forpinthed og de forlegne ansigter hos Sonja og Marja Dmitrijevna kunne greven tydeligt se, at noget var gået galt under hans fravær, men det var så forfærdeligt for ham at tænke, at noget vanærende var sket med hans elskede datter, og han satte så stor pris på sin egen muntre sindsro, at han undgik at spørge og forsøgte at overbevise sig selv om, at der ikke var sket noget særligt; og han var blot utilfreds med, at hendes upasselighed forsinkede deres hjemrejse til landet.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: Marya Dmitrievna, having found Sonya weeping in the corridor, made her confess everything, and intercepting the note to Natasha, she read it and went into Natasha's room with it in her hand.
"You shameless good-for-nothing!" said she. "I won't hear a word."

Pushing back Natasha, who looked at her with astonished but tearless eyes, she locked her in; and having ordered the yard porter to admit the persons who would be coming that evening but not to let them out again, and having told the footman to bring them up to her, she settled herself in the drawing room to wait for the abductors.

When Gabriel came to inform her that the men who had come had run away again, she rose frowning, and clasping her hands behind her paced through the rooms for a long time considering what she should do. Toward midnight she went to Natasha's room, fingering the key in her pocket. Sonya was sitting sobbing in the corridor. "Marya Dmitrievna, for God's sake let me in to her!" she begged, but Marya Dmitrievna unlocked the door and went in without answering... "Disgusting, abominable... In my house... horrid girl, hussy! I'm only sorry for her father!" she thought, trying to contain her fury. "Hard as it may be, I'll tell them all to hold their tongues and will hide it from the count." She entered the room with resolute steps. Natasha was lying on the sofa, her head hidden in her hands, and she didn't stir. She was in exactly the same position in which Marya Dmitrievna had left her.

"A nice girl! Very nice!" said Marya Dmitrievna. "Arranging meetings with lovers in my house! It's no use pretending — listen when I'm speaking to you!" And Marya Dmitrievna touched her arm. "Listen when I speak! You've disgraced yourself like the lowest of hussies. I'd treat you differently, but I'm sorry for your father, so I'll cover it up."
Natasha didn't change her position, but her whole body heaved with noiseless, convulsive sobs that choked her. Marya Dmitrievna glanced around at Sonya and sat down on the sofa beside Natasha.
"It's lucky for him that he escaped me; but I'll find him!" she said in her rough voice. "Do you hear what I'm saying or not?" she added.

She put her large hand under Natasha's face and turned it toward her. Both Marya Dmitrievna and Sonya were amazed at how Natasha looked. Her eyes were dry and glistening, her lips compressed, her cheeks sunken.
"Let me be!... What is it to me?... I shall die!" she muttered, wrenching herself from Marya Dmitrievna's hands with a violent effort and sinking back into her former position.

"Natalie!" said Marya Dmitrievna. "I want what's best for you. Lie still then, stay like that — I won't touch you. But listen. I won't tell you how guilty you are. You know that yourself. But when your father comes back tomorrow, what am I to tell him? Eh?"
Again Natasha's body shook with sobs.
"Suppose he finds out, and your brother, and your fiance?"
"I have no fiance — I've refused him!" cried Natasha.
"That's all the same," continued Marya Dmitrievna. "If they hear of this, will they let it pass? He, your father — I know him — if he challenges him to a duel, will that be all right? Eh?"
"Oh, leave me alone! Why have you interfered at all? Why? Why? Who asked you to?" shouted Natasha, raising herself on the sofa and looking at Marya Dmitrievna with fury.

"But what did you want?" cried Marya Dmitrievna, growing angry again. "Were you kept under lock and key? Who stopped him from coming to the house? Why carry you off as if you were some gypsy dancing girl?... Well, if he had carried you off... do you think they wouldn't have found him? Your father, or brother, or your fiance? And he's a scoundrel, a wretch — that's a fact!"
"He is better than any of you!" exclaimed Natasha, sitting up. "If you hadn't interfered... Oh, my God! What is it all? What is it? Sonya, why?... Go away!"
And she burst into sobs with the despairing intensity with which people mourn disasters they feel they have brought upon themselves. Marya Dmitrievna was about to speak again but Natasha cried out:
"Go away! Go away! You all hate and despise me!" and she threw herself back on the sofa.

Marya Dmitrievna went on lecturing her for some time, insisting that it must all be kept from her father and assuring her that nobody would know anything about it if only Natasha herself would promise to forget it all and not let anyone see that something had happened. Natasha didn't reply, nor did she sob any longer, but she grew cold and had a shivering fit. Marya Dmitrievna put a pillow under her head, covered her with two quilts, and brought her some lime-blossom tea herself, but Natasha didn't respond.
"Well, let her sleep," said Marya Dmitrievna, going out of the room, thinking Natasha had fallen asleep.
But Natasha was not asleep; with a pale face and wide-open eyes she stared straight ahead. All that night she didn't sleep or weep and didn't speak to Sonya, who got up and went to her several times.

The next day Count Rostov returned from his estate near Moscow in time for lunch, as he had promised. He was in very good spirits; the deal with the buyer was going well, and there was nothing to keep him any longer in Moscow, away from the countess whom he missed. Marya Dmitrievna met him and told him that Natasha had been very unwell the day before and that they had sent for the doctor, but that she was better now. Natasha hadn't left her room that morning. With tightly pressed, parched lips and dry, fixed eyes, she sat at the window, restlessly watching the people who drove past and quickly glancing around at anyone who entered the room. She was clearly expecting news of him — that he would come or would write to her.

When the count came to see her, she turned anxiously at the sound of a man's footstep, and then her face resumed its cold and hostile expression. She didn't even get up to greet him. "What is the matter with you, my angel? Are you ill?" asked the count.
After a moment's silence Natasha answered: "Yes, ill."

In reply to the count's anxious questions about why she was so dejected and whether anything had happened to her fiance, she assured him that nothing had happened and asked him not to worry. Marya Dmitrievna confirmed Natasha's assurances that nothing had happened. From the pretense of illness, from his daughter's distress, and from the embarrassed faces of Sonya and Marya Dmitrievna, the count saw clearly that something had gone wrong during his absence, but it was so terrible for him to think that anything disgraceful had happened to his beloved daughter, and he so valued his own cheerful peace of mind, that he avoided further questioning and tried to convince himself that nothing particularly bad had happened; and he was only annoyed that her illness delayed their return to the country.
